title: My MIL Assigned Seats and I Assigned the Receipts

parts.text: I sat in the torn vinyl chair because Gloria stuck my name there. Sunday dinner, assigned seats, roast chicken that tasted like lemon Pledge. I am forty-one, a teacher, professionally calm. Nate squeezed my knee like that counted as backup. Gloria tapped her glass. "We don't discuss money at dinner," she said, which meant mine. "Your fundraiser was cute. Nate's bonus should cover real things." I kept my parent-teacher smile. "The fundraiser bought paper." She laughed. "Paper. Adorable." The beagle, Biscuit, ate a green bean off the floor. Gloria pointed at an empty chair. "Slide down for your sister-in-law." I did not slide. Nate said, "Mom." Gloria said, "I paid for the patio." Last month she said Nate paid. After dessert she pulled me into the kitchen. "Until you have children, you're a guest." I opened the junk drawer for foil, the cheap stuff that rips, and found a Home Depot receipt on Nate's card. A sticky note in her handwriting said TELL THEM I PAID. Nate appeared. "What's that?" I held it up. Gloria's face did the parent-conference drop. She grabbed. I stepped back. The floral tin on the sideboard tipped and dumped more receipts into the chicken grease.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The tin dumped a paper trail she used to rewrite who paid, and the whole table is still waiting for pie.

social.video_title: Assigned seats, stolen patio credit — Part 1/2
social.description: Sunday dinner, a sticky-note chair, and a junk drawer that did not stay junk. I found a receipt with a note that said tell them I paid. What would you do at the table?

parts.text: Receipts slid into the gravy boat like they wanted an audience. I picked up three, all Nate's card, all relabeled in Gloria's looping script. "Bring the pie," my brother-in-law called. I brought pie and paper. I set both next to the salt shaker you have to stab. "Gloria paid for the patio," I said. "The bank says otherwise." Nate went pale, then angry in a direction that was not me. Gloria laughed too loud. "Family jokes." I read the sticky note. "Tell them I paid." Biscuit sneezed. My niece whispered, "Is this about chairs?" Nate said, "You told my cousins I couldn't afford my house." Gloria stood and knocked her wine. "I will not be audited in my home." I stayed in the torn vinyl chair because I was done sliding. Nate photographed the receipts and emailed himself, the simple thing he should have done years ago. I packed our blue-lid casserole dish that never seals. In the car he said, "I'm sorry." I said, "Don't be sorry. Stop letting her rewrite the bill." We skipped three Sundays. When we returned, there were no sticky notes, just a round table. I keep a photo of that note in a folder labeled seating chart. Petty. Fine.

social.video_title: I served pie with her fake receipts — Part 2/2
social.description: The gravy boat caught the paper trail and the whole table heard the sticky note. Assigned seating did not survive the audit. Would you have read it out loud?
